extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of mathematics; readers interested in ancient (Pythagorean/Greek) number theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains the ancient (Pythagorean and early Greek) definitions, classifications, constructions, and methods concerning numbers — units, parity, primes, perfect/friendly numbers, figured numbers, means and proportions, and related formulae. Focused on the conceptual and procedural standards used by classical authors (Aristotle, Euclid, Nicomachus, Theon, Iamblichus, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the unit (One)
rubrics_metrics.description: The One (unit) is often regarded as not itself a number; it is the beginning or principle of number rather than a numbered thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle: 'a measure is not the things measured, but the measure or the One is the beginning (or principle) of number.' Iamblichus and later sources record Pythagorean glosses calling the unit a 'limiting quantity' or 'confine between number and parts'. Chrysippus's 'multitude one' definition is noted and criticized as contradictory. Use this conception to distinguish 'unit' (principle) from 'number' in early Greek accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of number (classical variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number defined variously as 'a collection of units' (Thales), 'made number out of one' (Pythagoreans), 'determinate multitude' (Eudoxus), and 'a flow of quantity made up of units' (Nicomachus). Aristotle gives equivalent formulations like 'limited multitude', 'multitude of units', 'multitude measurable by one', etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text records multiple historically attributed definitions; when evaluating ancient doctrine, accept that 'number' was conceived either as aggregation of units or as a determinate/multitude concept. Different authors emphasize 'limit' (finite/determinate) or formation from units; these variants are equivalent for many purposes in the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of even and odd (ancient formulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient (Nicomachean/Pythagorean) definitions: an even number 'admits of being divided, by one and the same operation, into the greatest and the least parts ... into two halves'; an odd number 'cannot be so divided but is only divisible into two unequal parts.' Alternative version: even numbers can be divided both into two equal and into two unequal parts (except the dyad), while odd numbers, however divided, fall into two unequal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are descriptive/classificatory definitions rooted in factorization/partition properties. Note historical nuances: early thinkers did not necessarily include 2 as 'even' in the same sense, and definitions evolved over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even-odd taxonomy (even-even, even-odd, odd-even)
rubrics_metrics.description: A threefold subdivision used by Pythagoreans and Neo-Pythagoreans: 'even-even' (numbers repeatedly divisible by 2, i.e., 2^n), 'even-odd' (numbers that when halved once give an odd quotient, of form 2·(2m+1)), and 'odd-even' (numbers halved repeatedly leaving an odd quotient not equal to 1, of form 2^r·(2m+1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to classify numbers by the number of successive halvings possible and the parity of the ultimate quotient. The taxonomy underlies many Pythagorean distinctions and later Neo-Pythagorean refinements; it's the basis for distinguishing powers of two vs mixed parity forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of the unit and dyad with respect to parity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Pythagoreans held that the One arises from both kinds (odd and even) and is therefore 'even-odd' (partaking of both); alternative explanation: adding 1 to an even gives odd and adding 1 to odd gives even, so the unit partakes of both species. The dyad (2) was sometimes not originally regarded as a number and later treated as the only even prime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This entry records the historical interpretive stance about whether 1 and 2 are classified within the odd/even schema. Use with caution: sources differ (Aristotle, Theon, Neo-Pythagoreans) and later authors (Euclid) include 2 among primes while Neo-Pythagoreans often exclude even numbers from prime categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of prime (incomposite) and composite numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid: a prime number is 'that which is measured by a unit alone'; a composite is 'that which is measured by some number'. Additional notions: numbers 'prime to one another' (coprime) and 'composite to one another' (having a common measure). Neo-Pythagoreans later restrict prime/composite categories to odd numbers, often excluding 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical Euclidean definition (measured only by 1) is standard; note historical divergence where some schools excluded even numbers from these categories. Terminology variants (rectilinear, linear) are used to emphasize one-dimensionality of primes in early fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect numbers and their Euclidean construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect number: a number equal to the sum of its proper divisors (Euclid VII.Def.22); Euclid IX.36 gives a construction: if (2^p − 1) is prime then 2^(p−1)(2^p − 1) is perfect. Examples: 6, 28, 496, 8128, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nicomachus and Theon describe perfect, over-perfect (abundant), and defective (deficient) numbers and list known perfect numbers. Historical remarks about termination digits (6 or 8) and counts (Nicomachus knew four) are given; use Euclid's arithmetic construction as the standard generating law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendly (amicable) numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Two numbers are 'friendly' (amicable) when each equals the sum of the aliquot parts (proper divisors) of the other (example: 220 and 284). Tradition attributes discovery to Pythagoras; later mathematicians (Descartes, van Schooten, Euler) found more pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition and example provided; historical attributions and later enumerations (Euler's discovery of many pairs) are noted as context rather than prescriptive methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangular numbers (formation and formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangular numbers are formed by summing successive natural numbers beginning from 1: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2. The sequence corresponds to triangular dot arrangements; Pythagoreans likely knew this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via dot/pebble arrangements; Pythagorean lore connects triangular numbers to symbolic ideas (e.g., 1+2+3+4 = 10 as the 'perfect' Pythagorean number). Use geometric dot-arrangement arguments for proofs and visual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square numbers and gnomons (odd numbers as gnomons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Square numbers arise as sums of successive odd numbers: 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n+1) = (n+1)^2. The odd numbers added around a square are called gnomons; successive addition of these odd gnomons builds larger squares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents the dot/pebble geometric construction showing how odd gnomons produce squares; Aristotle's reference connects the notion to permanence of form. Use gnomon reasoning to demonstrate squares and their recurrence relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gnomon: history and generalized definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Gnomon originally an astronomical instrument (vertical stick), later an instrument for drawing right angles, and then the figure which, when added to a figure (like a square), produces a similar larger figure. Euclid generalizes gnomon to parallelograms and Heron to 'that which, when added to anything, makes the whole similar'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word's semantic shift from instrument to geometrical figure is traced. In number theory, 'gnomon' denotes the successive outer layers added to polygonal numbers; use the geometric meaning to interpret number-generation processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polygonal numbers and their gnomons
rubrics_metrics.description: Polygonal numbers (triangular, square, pentagonal, hexagonal, etc.) are formed by adding successive gnomons; for a k-gon the gnomonic sequence after 1 has common difference (k − 2). Examples: pentagonal gnomons 4,7,10,... (diff 3); hexagonal 5,9,13,... (diff 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general rule (common difference = n−2 for n-sided polygon) yields arithmetic progressions generating polygonal numbers; illustrative diagrams with dots demonstrate formation. Use for deriving closed formulas for polygonal numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right-angled triangles with integer sides (Pythagorean triples) and generation formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: Pythagorean triples are sets of three integers a,b,c with a^2 + b^2 = c^2. The text attributes generation formulas to Pythagoras and Plato: Pythagoras's method (if m is odd) yields (m^2 − 1)/2, m, (m^2 + 1)/2 kind of formations; Plato's formula (2m)^2 + (m^2 − 1)^2 = (m^2 + 1)^2 gives triples without parity restriction. Euclid's general solution uses parameters u and v (similar plane numbers) and parity conditions so that b and c are integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide both special (Pythagoras/Plato) and general (Euclid) constructions; Euclid's condition: for uv to be a square, u and v must be similar plane numbers, and u,v must be both odd or both even to yield integral b and c. Use parity constraints to ensure integer solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oblong numbers (pronic) and relation to triangular numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Oblong numbers are of form n(n+1) (product of two consecutive integers), equal to the sum 2 + 4 + ... + 2n, and are double triangular numbers. They are non-square numbers with 'sides' differing by 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pythagoreans associated oblongs with 'even' and 'unlimited' in their symbolic oppositions. Geometric dot-arrangements show oblongs as two equal triangular numbers; use to derive relations between triangular, square, and oblong sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations between squares and triangular numbers (identities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorems: any square number is the sum of two triangular numbers (with triangular sides differing by 1). Another identity: 8·T_n + 1 is a square (where T_n = n(n+1)/2), equivalently 8·(n(n+1)/2) + 1 is a perfect square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives geometric proofs via dot-figures and decompositions (divide a 2n+1 square into four oblong pieces plus 1). Use these identities in constructing number-theoretic relations and in proofs about triangular and square numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of proportion and the three classical means (arithmetic, geometric, harmonic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Pythagorean tradition recognizes three means: arithmetic mean (a + c = 2b), geometric mean (ac = b^2), and subcontrary/harmonic mean (in which proportional parts lead to harmonic progression). Archytas/Hippasus renamed the subcontrary 'harmonic'. These means were developed with musical theory connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions are given in terms of three-term sequences a>b>c and the relations between differences/ratios. Use these classical mean-definitions to link number ratios with musical intervals; the 'musical' or 'most perfect' four-term proportion (a:h = h:g = g:b) is also discussed as an application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended system of ten means (Pythagorean/Neo-Pythagorean developments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond the first three means, a system of ten means grew up (accounts vary on discoverers: Archytas, Hippasus, Eudoxus, Myonides, Euphranor). Nicomachus and Pappus list and give algebraic formulas for the ten; several lead to quadratic relations and imply knowledge of solving second-degree equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text supplies a table of formulae (Nicomachus/Pappus variants) and notes that Nos. 4–6 give quadratic equations, indicating geometric/algebraic methods for second-degree problems were known. Pappus shows how to parametrize many of these means from geometric progressions a, β, γ; use these relations as a historical source for early algebraic techniques.
